newsitem.title: UK: Lithuania plans repos in next weeks - c.banker.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania plans repos in next weeks - c.banker.

text.p: Lithuania plans to take first steps in the coming weeks to scrap its currency board but another Baltic state, Estonia, will stick with a similar system, central bankers said on Saturday.
Lithuania will begin a limited volume of repurchase tenders within the next two weeks as part of a plan to scrap the Baltic state's currency board system, central bank deputy head Jonas Niaura said.
"We should start now, maybe this week or next week," Niaura told Reuters after speaking at a Euromoney capital markets conference.
He said the repos, to be based on Treasury bills, would be limited to avoid damaging the central bank's function as lender of last resort.
Lithuania's right-of-centre government sparked investor concern after elections late last year when it said it would swiftly scrap the currency board.
Under the system, the central bank guarantees that it will keep one dollar in reserve for every four litas in circulation, freezing the exchange rate at that level.
But the government has since said the system will be gradually scrapped over two to three years, beginning with the repo auctions.

Niaura, in London for the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), said the gradual strategy had been agreed in consultation with the government and the International Monetary Fund.
"While the currency board arrangement had made a positive contribution ... Lithuania is now in a position to gradually move away from it," Niaura told the conference.

The currency board system has helped control money supply growth. Inflation was 13.1 percent last year, the lowest of the three Baltic states, and is likely to ease further in the next two years, Niaura said.

He said a fall in inflation and in interest rates, a build-up of external reserves and institutional improvements on the financial markets made it possible for the bank to widen its range of monetary policy instruments.
"Lithuania will proceed in this direction in a reliable manner and only after a period of adequate preparation to protect economic agents from destabilising surprises," he said.
Niaura said amendments to the currency law would be introduced next year to broaden the list of assets which could be used to back the litas.

In the last stage, not earlier than in 1999, the bank would consider whether to use a basket of European Union currencies alongside the dollar. "At this stage we envisage consideration of tagging the litas to the Euro," he said.
Estonia also uses a currency board system, which pegs its kroon currency at eight to the mark.

"Estonian experience has by and large shown the feasibility of using the exchange rate target as a nominal anchor for transitional economies like Estonia, at least if it is supported by sufficient fiscal and budgetary policies," central bank chief Vahur Kraft told the conference.
Some analysts have suggested Estonia might also have to scrap the system when Lithuania does but the finance ministry and central bank have denied this.
Kraft said that having a stable currency had made it easier to introduce world market prices in Estonia.
